reasons: The lake record is verified and identifies the case as Bond v. United States, court U.S. Supreme Court, year 2000.
The official citation 529 U.S. 334, parallel citations 120 S. Ct. 1462 and 146 L. Ed. 2d 365, and vendor-neutral citation 2000 U.S. LEXIS 2520 all match the lake record.

The opinion expressly applies the reasonable-expectation framework: it asks whether Bond exhibited an actual expectation of privacy and whether that expectation was one society is prepared to recognize as reasonable.
The holding turns on retained privacy in opaque luggage placed above Bond's seat, so the Reasonable Expectation of Privacy home role is supported.
residual_risks: The exact 'Key — Progeny' label is editorial, but the disclosed opinion strongly supports a key reasonable-expectation placement.

defect.evidence_quote: Indeed, it is undisputed here that petitioner possessed a privacy interest in his bag.

defect.problem: The disclosed record does not support placing Bond on an Abandonment home. Neither the lake record nor the opinion text classifies the case under abandonment or uses abandonment terminology; the opinion instead finds retained privacy despite public exposure/handling risk.
defect.proposed_fix: Remove the Abandonment home role unless another disclosed corpus source ties this public-exposure/lost-expectation analysis to the Abandonment doctrine.

reasons: The opinion supports Reasonable Expectation of Privacy, not abandonment.
Defaulting to refuted because the cross-doctrine Abandonment link cannot be verified from the disclosed files.
residual_risks: A separate Abandonment doctrine page might justify an editorial cross-link, but no such evidence is disclosed here.
reviewed.suggested_tightening: Replace with a disclosed, supported related concept such as public exposure or retained privacy if that taxonomy exists.

reasons: The opinion states: “This case presents the question whether a law enforcement officer’s physical manipulation of a bus passenger’s carry-on luggage violated the Fourth Amendment’s proscription against unreasonable searches. We hold that it did.”
The facts support the squeezing characterization: Agent Cantu “squeezed the soft luggage” and then “squeezed a green canvas bag.”
The tactile/visual distinction is supported by the opinion’s statement that physically invasive inspection is more intrusive than purely visual inspection.
residual_risks: The proposition should not be read to cover incidental ordinary handling; the opinion targets probing or exploratory tactile manipulation.
reviewed.suggested_tightening: Add “probing/exploratory” before “physical manipulation” for maximum fidelity.
